monument_name: Ṭīkā Bhairava at Bhelachẽ (c. mid-16th cent. CE)
description_en: Measuring 367 x 367 cm in size, the west-facing Ṭīkā Bhairava temple is located in the Bhelāchẽ Tol, to the north of the Durbar Square of Patan. Ṭīkā Bhairava is also known as Unmatta Bhairava or Mahā Bhairava. The Bhelāchẽ Tol was named after this temple; its name derives from the Nevārī wordbhelā,meaning Bhairava, and'hẽ,meaning house.The main entry gate to the temple is to the west and is flanked by two guardian lions, which in turn have two metal flags between them. In front of the main entry, one can find a brick-paved space that contains several small objects. One of these is a stone Padmapatra, sitting almost at the centre and in line with the main entrance. One can also find a stone trough of an abandonedjarḥũhiti, which measures 50 cm in width and 173 cm in length. The lower banner on its right-hand side is broken.The Ṭīkā Bhairava temple is a three-storey pagoda-style temple, and stands on a low stone base. All three roofs of the temple are made of copper sheets. Above the entrance is agaruḍa toraṇashowing an image of Bhairava with eight hands. Bhairava is holdinggajacarma, ḍamaru, katṛandkapālawith his right hands, andgajacarma, khaṭvāṅgaandnaramuṇḍawith his left. The last hand is in abinduposition. Bhairava is at the centre of thetoraṇaand is flanked by Gaṇeśa and Kumāra. Behind thetoraṇais a window with a wall painting of Khyā on its left and an image of Kavã on its right. Below the second roof, in front of the window on the western side, one can find a woodentoraṇawith images of similar deities painted in different colors. At the top of the temple is a pinnacle with serpents in its four corners. A banner hangs down from the pinnacle to the bottom of the temple's first roof on the western side.The sanctum is a colonnaded space with 12 octagonal columns standing in three bays on each side. The central area within this space is demarcated by a 2.1m long wall of 70 cm thickness and two timber posts. Together, these form a square space; the main image of the deity, which faces to the west, is attached to the wall. However, the sanctum does not contain a stone image of the main deity. Instead, there is a metalśivaliṅga, with an image of Bhairava painted on the wall behind it. To the left of theśivaliṅgais a stone image of Gaṇeśa with four arms, and to its right hand side is a stone image of Kumāra, also with four arms.Uutside, the temple has twenty struts supporing the lowest roof. The four corner struts contain images ofśārdūla, while the other 16 struts display images of the Eight Mātṛkās and Eight Bhairavas. Alongside this, the struts to the west also contain images of Rudra Bhairava mounted on a human being, Māheśvarī, Unmatta Bhairava mounted on a lion, and Brahmāyaṇī. The southern struts display Bhairava mounted on a human being, Mahālakṣmī, a Bhairava riding on a horse, and Cāmuṇḍā. To the east, the struts contain images of Bhairava mounted on a bull, Indrāyaṇī, Kapāla Bhairava riding on a snake, and Vārāhī. Finally, the northern struts display images of Bhairava mounted on a Garuḍa, Vaiṣṇavī, Pracaṇḍa Bhairava mounted on a boar, and Kumārī (Tachikawa2004,17-19).In the temple area are a bell, ajarũhiṭī, a small stone image of Basāhā and an aniconic stone image of Ajimā.According toPruscha(1975, 176) this temple was built in 1541 but no inscription could be found  to provide evidence of this date. Mention of this temple is, however, made inKīrtipatākā, a text composed by Kunu Śarmā. It describes images of gods drawn on the walls of the temple (see inNaraharinātha1961, 12).
monument_assessment: Slightly damaged (minor damages such as minor cracks, plants, missing stones in plinths)
references: Sources and references Sources Inscription of NS 661 ( Pruscha 1975, 171)

historical_events.event_description: According to a lost inscription, Jñāna Singh Natu donated this temple in NS 661 (Pruscha1975, 171).
According to a lost inscription, the lions of this temple were donated in NS 841 (Pruscha1975, 176).

The gold-coated third roof and the pinnacle were fixed on the top of the temple. This donation was made by Gangā Lakṣmī Prajāpati alongside his younger brother Pādauwa, his sons Bekhā Singh, Dhija Bīr, Kula Bīr, and his grandson Dhijamā.
Pūrṇa Lāl Avāle donated thetoraṇaabove the entrance.
Two brass flags were donated and fixed on either side of the entrance by Pūrṇa Lāl Avāle
Gilding of the entrance thanks to Pūrṇa Lāl Avāle
Donation of thepatāḥwhich hangs down from the pinnacle
In the memory of their deceased grandfather Gopāl, father Lāl and mother Dyālakṣmī, Indralāl and Chirkāji Avāle replaced the tiles on the second roof with copper plates.
